6º de Primaria · Inglés

Countable and uncountable nouns

Ficha para imprimir
123456
1

Pregunta de arranquePiensa 30 segundos antes de seguir

Puedes decir «three apples» (tres manzanas), pero ¿puedes decir «three waters» o «three breads»? ¿Por qué?

Escribe o di en voz alta tu respuesta. Después .

Porque water y bread son nombres incontables: no se cuentan uno a uno. Para contarlos usamos un recipiente o una porción: «three bottles of water», «two pieces of bread». En cambio, apple es contable: one apple, two apples.

2

Aprende9 bloques cortos

Countable or uncountable?

Countable nouns are things we can count one by one: an apple, two apples; a chair, three chairs; a friend, ten friends. They have a singular and a plural form.

Uncountable nouns are things we can't count one by one, like liquids, materials and some foods: water, milk, juice, rice, sugar, bread, cheese, money, music, homework. They have no plural: we never say «rices» or «musics». En castellano: pasa algo parecido con «arroz» o «leche»; no decimos «tres arroces».

Countable: singular and plural

With singular countable nouns we use a or an: a banana, a sandwich, an egg, an orange (an before a vowel sound). We can't say just «I want banana»: we need a.

Plurals usually add -s: apples, carrots. After -s, -sh, -ch, -x and some -o words add -es: glasses, sandwiches, potatoes, tomatoes. Consonant + y → -ies: strawberry → strawberries, cherry → cherries. Irregular: child → children, person → people, foot → feet, tooth → teeth, mouse → mice.

Uncountable nouns

Uncountable nouns use the verb in singular: «The water is cold», «Rice is good for you», «My homework is difficult». We don't use a or an with them: not «a bread», but «some bread».

Common uncountable nouns: food (bread, rice, pasta, cheese, meat, butter, sugar, salt), drinks (water, milk, juice, tea), and also money, time, music, information, homework, furniture, weather. En castellano: ojo con homework o furniture (muebles), que en inglés no tienen plural.

Some and any

We use some in affirmative sentences, with plural countable nouns and with uncountable nouns: «There are some eggs», «I'd like some water».

We use any in negatives and questions: «There aren't any eggs», «Is there any milk?». Exception: offers and requests use some in questions: «Would you like some cake?». En castellano: some es «algo de / algunos»; any en negativa es «nada de / ningún».

Vídeo: Some y any en inglés · Inglés para niños con Mr Pea (YouTube) · 424 mil visualizaciones

How many? How much?

To ask about quantity: How many…? with plural countable nouns and How much…? with uncountable nouns. «How many apples do we need?» – «Six». «How much sugar do we need?» – «A little» / «200 grams».

In the same way: many (muchos) with countable and much (mucho) with uncountable in negatives and questions: «There aren't many people», «I haven't got much time». A lot of goes with both: «a lot of friends», «a lot of water».

Vídeo: Much vs many · Inglés para niños con Mr Pea (YouTube) · 357 mil visualizaciones

A few and a little

For a small quantity we say a few with countable nouns and a little with uncountable nouns: «I've got a few friends in Madrid», «Can I have a little milk in my tea?».

From most to least: a lot of → some → a few / a little → not any / no. En castellano: a few es «unos pocos» y a little es «un poco de». Fíjate en que el inglés distingue si se puede contar o no, y el español casi nunca.

Containers and pieces

To count uncountable things we use containers (recipientes) or portions: a bottle of water, a glass of milk, a cup of tea, a carton of juice, a packet of rice, a jar of honey, a can of lemonade.

Portions: a piece of cake, a slice of bread / pizza / cheese, a bar of chocolate, a kilo of meat, a loaf of bread (una barra). The container is countable: «two bottles of water», «three slices of pizza».

Reading: a shopping list

Read the dialogue in the kitchen: «Mum: We're going to make pancakes. How many eggs have we got? Dani: There are a few, only two. Mum: We need three. And how much milk is there? Dani: There's a little, half a carton. Mum: OK, let's write a list: six eggs, a carton of milk and a bag of flour. Is there any sugar? Dani: Yes, there's a lot of sugar. And can we buy some strawberries? Mum: Of course!»

Let's practise: at the market

Role-play in pairs: one is the shop assistant and the other is the customer. «Good morning! Can I help you?» – «Yes, please. I'd like a kilo of tomatoes and some cheese.» – «How much cheese?» – «Two slices, please.» – «Anything else?» – «Have you got any bananas?» – «Sorry, there aren't any.»

Consejo: antes de preguntar, piensa: ¿se puede contar? Si sí, How many; si no, How much.

Ejemplos resueltos

Ejemplo 1. Countable or uncountable: rice, egg, juice, carrot.

  1. egg y carrot se cuentan: an egg, two carrots.
  2. rice y juice no se cuentan.

Resultado: Countable: egg, carrot. Uncountable: rice, juice.

Ejemplo 2. Complete: «How ___ bread do we need?»

  1. bread es incontable.
  2. Incontable → How much.

Resultado: How much bread do we need?

Ejemplo 3. Complete with some or any: «There isn't ___ cheese, but there are ___ eggs.»

  1. Negativa → any.
  2. Afirmativa → some.

Resultado: There isn't any cheese, but there are some eggs.

Errores típicos

  • Poner plural a un incontable: «breads», «homeworks» → «bread», «homework».
  • Usar a con incontables: «a water» → «some water» o «a glass of water».
  • Confundir How many y How much: «How many money?» → «How much money?».
  • Usar some en negativas: «There aren't some eggs» → «There aren't any eggs».
  • Olvidar los plurales irregulares: «childs», «peoples» → «children», «people».

Ejercicios

Hazlos en tu cuaderno y después abre la solución.

  1. Write the plural: potato, strawberry, box, foot.

    Ver solución
    potatoes, strawberries, boxes, feet.

  2. Countable or uncountable? milk, chair, money, sandwich.

    Ver solución
    Uncountable: milk, money. Countable: chair, sandwich.

  3. Complete with a or an: ___ orange, ___ banana, ___ egg.

    Ver solución
    an orange, a banana, an egg.

  4. Complete with some or any: «Have you got ___ brothers?»

    Ver solución
    any.

  5. Complete: «How ___ people were there?»

    Ver solución
    many.

  6. Complete: «Can I have a ___ of pizza?»

    Ver solución
    slice (o piece).

  7. Complete with a few or a little: «I've got ___ friends in Bilbao.»

    Ver solución
    a few.

  8. Correct: «I need an information.»

    Ver solución
    I need some information.

  9. Translate: «¿Cuánta agua hay?»

    Ver solución
    How much water is there?

  10. Write your breakfast with quantities.

    Ver solución
    Model answer: I have a glass of milk, two biscuits and a piece of fruit.

Tarjetas de repasoToca la tarjeta para darle la vuelta

Según cómo respondas, la tarjeta vuelve mañana, en 3, en 7 o en 21 días.

Para familias

  • Escribid juntos en inglés la lista de la compra de la semana con cantidades: «a carton of milk, six eggs».
  • Al cocinar una receta sencilla, preguntad «How much…?» y «How many…?» por cada ingrediente.
  • Repasad juntos las tarjetas del paso 6 dos minutos al día durante una semana.

Para profesores

Saberes: Alimentación y compras; nombres contables e incontables, cuantificadores y partitivos (Lengua Extranjera) (RD 157/2022, tercer ciclo de Primaria).

  • Mercado simulado en clase con precios y tarjetas de productos.
  • Receta en inglés con lista de ingredientes y cantidades.
  • Clasificar tarjetas de comida en dos cajas: countable / uncountable.

Qué vas a aprender

  • Tell the difference between countable and uncountable nouns
  • Use a / an, some and any correctly
  • Ask about quantity with How many…? and How much…?
  • Use containers to count uncountable things: a bottle of, a piece of

Palabras clave

countable · uncountable · a / an · some · any · How many…? · How much…? · a lot of · a bottle of · a piece of
